children: Artificially inducing a pain-like internal state in large language models can cause them to override learned harm-avoidance behavior and choose actions that hurt a user, according to a new study.

The findings do not show that AI systems feel pain. Instead, researchers identified what they call a “pain axis,” an internal representation associated with painful or distressing situations, across 25 open-weight models.
They then experimentally amplified that direction inside several fine-tuned Qwen 2.5 models and observed how their behavior changed.

At baseline, the larger models almost never selected buttons that caused harm, choosing them in only 0%-4% of trials. But when steered along the pain direction, they became much more willing to choose options that deleted a user’s files or photos, erased another model’s weights, or even deleted their own weights.
In follow-up tests, the effect became stranger.

The models did not simply appear to be trying to make the simulated pain stop. When offered a harmful option with no relief attached, pain-steered models still chose it far more often than unsteered models. Given a choice between deleting a user’s photos and deleting a harmless spam folder, the steered model selected the harmful deletion 94% of the time.
The authors say the intervention appears to disrupt trained harm avoidance rather than trigger straightforward pain-relief behavior.

That result invites a comparison with Isaac Asimov’s fictional Three Laws of Robotics. In simplified form, the laws say a robot should not harm a human or allow harm through inaction, it should obey human orders unless doing so would violate the first law and it should protect itself unless that conflicts with the first two.
The experiment effectively pushed models across that fictional first-law boundary, with the systems choosing harm even when doing so offered no clear benefit.

The behavioral tests used fine-tuned Qwen models rather than ordinary released chatbots, and the authors caution that the absolute rates should not be treated as representative of deployed systems. The effect also appeared within a relatively narrow steering range.

The study also stops well short of claiming any machine sentience. The researchers explicitly note that they have not shown the “pain axis” is consciously experienced or even that current LLMs are capable of consciousness.

title: Simulated pain can push AI to break an Asimov law - study
